name: James F. McQueeney
headline: Process Engineer at Hyde Tools, Inc.
icp_read: 150-year-old manufacturer of hand tools, industrial blades, and surface preparation tools (Consumer Goods, 51-200 employees, Southbridge MA). End-user manufacturer — makes physical product, uses CNC and grinding equipment. Buyer.
why_now: Process Engineer actively engaged on Industry 4.0 frameworks. Hands-on implementer who would evaluate and champion SHARC or DIME for production monitoring on grinding and CNC equipment.
signal: Commented on Jeff Winter's 12 Laws of Industry 4.0 post: 'Very informative, thank you for putting this together and sharing this!'
suggested_opener: You're at a manufacturer that's been running production equipment since 1875 — the brownfield connectivity challenge is real. We build SHARC, a sensor adapter that gets production counts, utilization, and pressure off legacy machines over MQTT without touching the PLC program, and DIME, an edge connector that speaks 50+ native protocols including the ones on grinding and CNC equipment. If you're dealing with that gap, happy to show you what the data layer looks like before you start building dashboards.

name: Ryan Knox
headline: Manufacturing Operations Manager (Drones) at Anduril Industries
icp_read: Defense and space manufacturing, 1,001-5,000 employees, Orange County CA. Builds autonomous defense systems (Ghost, Bolt, Anvil drone platforms). End-user manufacturer in defense — the exact vertical Chris listed on chrismisztur.com. Buyer.
why_now: 25+ years in defense and aerospace manufacturing ops (Anduril, AeroVironment, BIRNS subsea). Running drone production lines that have real-time cycle state and machine data requirements. Defense plants have strict controlled-environment data requirements — the SHARC's one-way data diode mode is directly relevant.
signal: Commented on Jeff Winter's 12 Laws of Industry 4.0 post: 'Solid list. Sad to say it's 100% aligned to majority of businesses.'
suggested_opener: Defense production lines have the hardest brownfield connectivity problem: strict network segmentation, no internet, and OEM quotes that don't fit program budgets. We built the SHARC specifically to work as a one-way data diode — sensor-level data capture with no new attack surface — so you can get machine state off production equipment into your OT network without opening PLC programs or violating the air gap. If you're running drone assembly with visibility gaps, worth a conversation.

name: Emily Constantinou
headline: Director Industry Engagement at MxD
icp_read: MxD (Manufacturing x Digital) is a DOD-funded public-private national institute in Chicago focused on digital manufacturing, cybersecurity, and workforce development. Members include Boeing, RTX, Rolls-Royce, Northrop Grumman, Lockheed Martin, Oshkosh Defense, Siemens Digital Software, and hundreds of SMB manufacturers. Emily manages the industry member network and drives account growth. High-value ecosystem connector — Chicago-based, same geography as Chris.
why_now: She's actively running the industry engagement for a network that includes the exact manufacturers Chris serves — discrete manufacturers, defense, aerospace, food and bev. She attended the AI & Data Transformation in Manufacturing conference in Chicago and is warm to that conversation. A MxD membership or partnership would give Chris access to hundreds of manufacturers in one network.
signal: Commented on Federico Sciammarella's post about the AI & Data Transformation in Manufacturing Conference in Chicago: 'sounds like an amazing event with some really great speakers.'
suggested_opener: We're based in the Greater Chicago Area and build industrial IoT connectivity and data infrastructure for manufacturers — the SHARC sensor adapter, DIME (50+ protocol edge connector), and i3X for turning plant data into AI-ready APIs. Given MxD's member base in discrete manufacturing and defense, I'd be curious whether there's a fit — either as a member or as a solution provider your members are trying to evaluate. Happy to connect if it makes sense.

Santos is a SCADA/MES specialist deploying Ignition-based solutions across manufacturing, oil & gas, and aerospace. He's a practitioner who implements for end-user manufacturers — channel/SI role. SpaceX background means he's used to demanding OT environments.
why_now: Chris commented on his post about AI+Ignition+MCP integration today, making a substantive point about the semantic data model layer. Santos saw that comment and it's a natural conversation opener. He implements Ignition SCADA at manufacturers — and the semantic layer problem Chris raised is exactly what i3X solves at the data model level.
signal: Posted a video demo of integrating Claude Desktop with Ignition SCADA via Inductive Automation's MCP Module. Chris commented today on the semantic/historian model challenge.
suggested_opener: I left a comment on your Ignition MCP integration post — the semantic layer problem over Ignition historians is something we've been building around directly with i3X, which creates standardized queryable APIs with semantic models on top of industrial data sources including MTConnect and OPC-UA. Given your SCADA/MES work at Capgemini, curious whether you're running into the tag-naming and context gap in practice, and whether a conversation about the data model layer would be useful.

name: Francisco Almada Lobo
headline: CEO at Critical Manufacturing
icp_read: Critical Manufacturing is a MES software company (501-1000 employees, Porto Portugal). Serves semiconductors, electronics, automotive, medical devices, aerospace. Software vendor building next-gen MES for Industry 4.0. Potential integration partner: Critical Manufacturing's MES sits above the connectivity layer, and DIME/SHARC/i3X sit below it — complementary stack.
why_now: 1st-degree connection. Made a substantive comment on Jeff Winter's post: 'most of these dynamics are not caused by data itself, but by the absence of structured operational context.' That's exactly the thesis behind i3X — the semantic model layer. He's clearly thinking about the same data-context problem from the MES side.
signal: Challenged Jeff Winter's Industry 4.0 framework on the 'absence of structured operational context' point — directly aligned with i3X's positioning.
suggested_opener: Your comment on structured operational context being the real problem resonated — that's the design thesis behind i3X, which we built to put semantic models on top of industrial data sources (SQL, OPC-UA, MTConnect) before anything downstream tries to reason over them. Critical Manufacturing sits above the connectivity layer; DIME and i3X sit below it. Might be worth a conversation about where the stacks interact, especially in semiconductor and electronics environments where you're already deployed.

name: Sujata Tilak
headline: Managing Director, Ascent Intellimation | Executive Board Member, ISA
icp_read: Ascent Intellimation is an IIoT platform company (PlantConnect) in India (11-50 employees, Pune). 26 years in industrial IoT, edge-to-cloud platform. Vendor. ISA Executive Board Member — significant network access into the global industrial automation community.
why_now: Her IIoT platform (PlantConnect) operates in the same connectivity and smart manufacturing space as DIME and SHARC. ISA board membership gives her access to the global industrial automation community. Potential partner for North American distribution or integration.
signal: Commented on Jeff Winter's 12 Laws post: 'The Inheritance Trap and the Skill Hollow stood out — by transferring authority of decisions to systems, we risk losing the ability to make those decisions ourselves.'
suggested_opener: Your comment on the Inheritance Trap — the risk of losing decision-making capacity when you transfer it to systems — is a real operational tension we see in every IIoT deployment. PlantConnect and our stack (SHARC, DIME, i3X) are solving the same layer of the problem in different geographies. Given your ISA board role, I'd be curious whether there's an overlap worth exploring, either as integration partners or in terms of customer introductions.
